summary: Psalm 56 begins with a speaker under constant human pressure, asking God for mercy while enemies attack, twist words, and watch for a chance to take his life. The psalm moves from fear to trust, from a plea for judgment to confidence that God notices wandering and tears. It closes with vows and thank offerings because God has delivered the speaker from death and kept his feet from falling.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how a psalm can hold fear, accusation, trust, and gratitude in one prayer. In Book II of Psalms, it is one of the David-associated poems that teaches threatened people how to speak honestly before God without pretending danger is unreal.

context.author: Many psalms are associated with David, and this heading links the poem to David when the Philistines seized him in Gath; the exact historical origin and force of such headings are debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as public and private prayer.
context.date: The Psalms are a collection formed over time; a precise date for Psalm 56 cannot be established from its wording and heading alone.
context.setting: The heading names Gath and the Philistines; the poem itself speaks from fear, pursuit, slander, wandering, and trust in God.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer, with repeated lines of trust and praise, complaint against enemies, and a thanksgiving-shaped conclusion.

outline.heading: Cry for mercy under attack
outline.note: The speaker asks God for mercy because many enemies attack, oppress, and want to swallow him up.

outline.heading: Fear answered by trust
outline.note: Fear is named directly, but the speaker answers it by trusting God and asking what flesh can do.

outline.heading: Enemies twist words and stalk life
outline.note: The danger becomes more specific: enemies distort his speech, conspire, lurk, and are eager to take his life, so he asks God to cast them down.

outline.heading: God counts sorrow and turns enemies back
outline.note: The speaker says God counts his wanderings, keeps his tears, and will make enemies turn back when he calls.

outline.heading: Renewed trust and praise
outline.note: The earlier confession returns with added repetition: he praises God's word, trusts God, and refuses fear.

outline.heading: Vows after deliverance
outline.note: The psalm ends with vows, thank offerings, and the reason for them: God has delivered the speaker from death and kept his feet from falling.

keyVerses.text: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter's simplest statement of its movement: fear is real, but it is answered by trust in God.

keyVerses.text: In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?
keyVerses.why: The verse joins praise, trust, and courage, and it introduces the question repeated later in the psalm.

keyVerses.text: You count my wanderings. You put my tears into your container. Aren’t they in your book?
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the chapter's claim that the speaker's suffering is noticed and remembered by God.

keyVerses.text: For you have delivered my soul from death, and prevented my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of the living.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse gives the reason for the promised thank offerings: deliverance from death and preservation for life before God.

questions.question: What situation does the heading give for this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says this is a poem by David, connected with the time when the Philistines seized him in Gath. Headings are ancient parts of the received book, but their exact historical relation to a poem is debated. So the heading matters, but it should not be treated as a modern-style byline with every question settled.

questions.question: What does the speaker mean by saying enemies want to “swallow me up”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the first two verses as an image for destructive pressure from enemies. The chapter explains it with nearby terms: they attack, oppress, fight proudly, twist words, conspire, lurk, and seek his life. The image is poetic, not a separate event from the rest of the danger described.

questions.question: Is the speaker fearless?
questions.answer: No. Verse 3 begins, “When I am afraid,” so the psalm does not deny fear. The change is that fear becomes the occasion for trust: “I will put my trust in you.” Verses 4 and 11 then state, “I will not be afraid,” as a confession grounded in trust, not as a claim that danger has vanished.

questions.question: What is meant by “flesh” in verse 4?
questions.answer: In this verse, “flesh” is paired with the question, “What can flesh do to me?” Verse 11 repeats the idea with “man,” which shows that the speaker is contrasting human threat with trust in God. The point is not that people can do nothing harmful, since the psalm plainly describes real danger; it is that human power is not the final measure of the speaker's hope.

questions.question: What are the enemies doing besides physical attack?
questions.answer: They twist the speaker's words, think against him for evil, conspire, lurk, and watch his steps. The danger is social and verbal as well as physical. The chapter presents hostile speech and surveillance as part of the threat against his life.

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask God to cast down the peoples in anger?
questions.answer: Verse 7 is a hard verse because it asks for judgment: “In anger cast down the peoples, God.” The psalm connects that request to enemies acting by iniquity and seeking escape. Readers differ on how such prayers should be used later: some emphasize handing judgment to God instead of taking revenge, while others struggle with the severity of the request.

questions.question: What does the image of tears in God’s container say?
questions.answer: Verse 8 pictures God as counting the speaker's wanderings and preserving his tears. The point is that suffering is not ignored or lost. The verse uses intimate imagery for divine attention, but it does not explain the mechanics of a literal record.

questions.question: What does “God is for me” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The phrase appears after the speaker says his enemies will turn back in the day he calls. In this chapter, it means the speaker trusts God to hear, remember, and act on his behalf. It is stated as confidence within danger, not as a claim that the speaker has never been threatened.

questions.question: Why does the psalm end with vows and thank offerings?
questions.answer: The speaker says, “Your vows are on me, God,” and promises thank offerings. Verse 13 gives the reason: God has delivered his soul from death and prevented his feet from falling. The ending turns the earlier plea into public gratitude for preservation and continued life before God.

glossary.def: A figure named in the heading, indicating that the psalm is connected with musical or worship performance, though the exact ancient performance setting is not explained in the chapter.
The tune named in the heading. The title is preserved, but the melody itself is not known from this chapter alone.
The place named in the heading where the Philistines seized David. The poem itself does not narrate the event; it prays from the pressure associated with it.
Promises or obligations the speaker says are upon him before God, linked here with giving thank offerings after deliverance.
Offerings the speaker promises to give to God in response to deliverance described in the final verse.
